items.title: ag-ui-protocol/ag-ui
items.content:
AG-UI: the Agent-User Interaction Protocol. Bring Agents into Frontend Applications.

AG-UI is an open, lightweight, event-based protocol that standardizes how AI agents connect to user-facing applications.

Agents don't fit the request/response model. They stream tokens, call tools mid-response, update shared state, pause for a human, and spawn subagents, and every framework does it differently. AG-UI replaces that custom wiring with one bi-directional event stream: the agent emits typed events, and any client can render them, no matter which framework built the agent. The same agent can power a web app, a mobile app, a terminal, or Slack.

The protocol now has a stable, frozen specification backed by a JSON Schema, and the TypeScript, Python, and .NET SDKs are generated from it. 1.0 is backwards compatible in both directions: 0.x agents work with 1.0 clients and vice versa. What changed → · Migration guide →

The CLI scaffolds a frontend (CopilotKit on Next.js, or a terminal client) wired to the agent framework you pick:

npx create-ag-ui-app@latest

Then follow the printed next steps. The generated templates call OpenAI, so set your key before :

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."

AG-UI is one of three open, complementary agentic protocols. gives agents tools and context, lets agents work with other agents, and brings agents to users. A single agent often uses all three, and AG-UI can front agents that speak MCP or A2A. Read more →

They work together. A2UI, MCP Apps, and Open-JSON-UI are : they describe what UI an agent wants to show. AG-UI is the that carries those payloads, along with everything else, between the agent and the app. Learn more →

AG-UI is adopted by Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Oracle, and built into most agent frameworks. Every framework below has a live demo in the Dojo.

Full list of integrations

Features: what you can build

Each building block maps to events in the spec, and each has a live demo in the AG-UI Dojo.

Token-by-token messages across multi-turn sessions, with cancel and resume
Agents render typed components, or declarative UI with A2UI and MCP Apps
A typed store the agent and app both read and write, synced with snapshots and JSON Patch deltas
The agent calls tools that run in the app, and gets the result back
Runs end with an outcome; the user approves, edits, or rejects, and the next run resumes
Show the agent's reasoning as it works, including encrypted reasoning round-trips
Nested delegation, with every event attributed to the subagent run that produced it
Images, audio, video, and documents in user input and tool results

Tool output streaming, backend tool rendering, activity progress, token usage, and custom events are covered in the docs. Here's a quick tour of the Dojo:

Your app starts a run by sending the agent a single : the conversation, the tools the frontend offers, shared state, and context. The agent answers with a stream of typed events from eight families: run lifecycle, text messages, tool calls, state, reasoning, activity, subagents, and custom events (full list). Only the run lifecycle is required, so a minimal agent emits a handful of events and grows from there.

AG-UI 1.0 defines 31 event types in eight families. See the spec for every field.

(JSON Patch)
REASONING_ENCRYPTED_VALUE

AG-UI was created by CopilotKit and is developed in the open with the community.

items.title: dream-num/univer
items.content:
Build your own AI office with Univer Office SDK. Bring editing, calculation, collaboration, and file processing into your product for people and AI agents. Built on an extensible open-source core.

Start with open-source Sheets and Docs, then connect your own application or agent.

is an Office SDK for building Office applications inside your own product. It provides Office editing, calculation, collaboration, and file processing for people and existing agents, using your data and permissions. The product family covers spreadsheets, documents, presentations, relational tables, canvases, and PDFs.

Univer Office SDK has three parts:

  • is the foundation: content models, editing, rendering, formula calculation, and Facade APIs (application-facing APIs). Compose its plugins into an embedded editor or your own Office application, and reuse the content models, commands, and calculation for Headless processing without an interactive editor.
  • adds backend services for real-time collaboration, edit history, and Office file import and export.
  • connects Office capabilities to existing agents and workflows, with content tools, execution, and review integrations.

This repository provides the Web SDK's core architecture and engine implementations under Apache-2.0: content models and snapshot formats, plugin and dependency management, the command system, formula and rendering engines, Facade APIs, UI foundation, and Sheets and Docs editing capabilities. Commercial Web SDK plugins, Server SDK, and commercial AI SDK extensions are distributed and licensed separately.

Agents can use the same open-source APIs; your application supplies the model and tool orchestration. The quotation example demonstrates editing, calculation, and saving without an AI SDK dependency.

Sheets · Editing and layoutCell styles, merged cells, in-cell rich text, freeze panes, floating images, and undo/redo.
Sheets · Data and calculationFormulas, defined names, filtering, sorting, data validation, conditional formatting, hyperlinks, comments, and find and replace.
Rich-text editing, paragraph formatting, lists, hyperlinks, comments, and drawing integration.

Features are composed through plugins and presets; the quick start uses only the . Images use the corresponding drawing plugins. See the feature comparison for detailed open-source and commercial coverage.

The demos below showcase the wider , including commercial capabilities. They show more than the default open-source setup; see open source and commercial extensions for scope.

🚀 Build on the open-source foundation

Use the open-source foundation
Add an editable Office surface to your application or agent product, and connect your data through Facade APIs.
Process content without an editorReuse content plugins, models, commands, and calculation in Node.js for editing, snapshots, and automated tasks.
Develop custom features or editorsReuse the engines, UI components, plugin boundaries, dependency injection, and command/undo systems. Follow existing features to extend Sheets and Docs or develop your own editors.

Coordinate edits and undo/redo across features. Inserting a row inside a filter range changes both the base content and the filter range; undo needs to restore both. Each feature supplies its own changes and undo data, and the command composes their execution and history. The architecture walkthrough explains how to extend these editing workflows.

Quick start: an open-source spreadsheet editor

In a browser application using a bundler such as Vite:

pnpm add @univerjs/presets @univerjs/preset-sheets-core

Create the container before initializing Univer:

<div id="app" style="height: 100vh"></div>

import { UniverSheetsCorePreset } from '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core'
import UniverPresetSheetsCoreEnUS from '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core/locales/en-US'
import { createUniver, LocaleType, mergeLocales } from '@univerjs/presets'
import '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core/lib/index.css'

const { univerAPI } = createUniver({
  locale: LocaleType.EN_US,
  locales: {
    [LocaleType.EN_US]: mergeLocales(UniverPresetSheetsCoreEnUS),
  },
  presets: [
    UniverSheetsCorePreset({
      container: 'app',
    }),
  ],
})

univerAPI.createWorkbook({})

Your page now contains a spreadsheet editor. Use the returned to work with its content. This example uses open-source packages and needs no commercial Univer license or Server SDK.

For component frameworks, retain the instance returned by and call when the component unmounts. See the lifecycle guide.

Presets compose plugins and register their Facade APIs. For manual control, see the Plugin Mode example below. The installation guide covers both modes, peer dependencies, and framework integrations.

Keep coordinated packages on the same version. Commercial packages must use the matching release line; independently released packages such as icons follow their declared compatibility. See the API Stability Policy.

Connect your application to editable content

Facade APIs are the application-facing interface to workbooks, worksheets, and ranges. Continue from the quick start to populate a quotation, update a quantity from application code, and read the recalculated total:

// Wait for formula controllers before editing a newly created workbook.
await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
  if (univerAPI.getCurrentLifecycleStage() >= univerAPI.Enum.LifecycleStages.Steady) {
    resolve()
    return
  }
  const listener = univerAPI.addEvent(univerAPI.Event.LifeCycleChanged, ({ stage }) => {
    if (stage === univerAPI.Enum.LifecycleStages.Steady) {
      listener.dispose()
      resolve()
    }
  })
})

const workbook = univerAPI.getActiveWorkbook()!
const sheet = workbook.getActiveSheet()

sheet.getRange('A1:D4').setValues([
  ['Item', 'Quantity', 'Unit price', 'Amount'],
  ['Seats', 2, 25, '=B2*C2'],
  ['Support', 1, 100, '=B3*C3'],
  ['Total', '', '', '=SUM(D2:D3)'],
])

// An application control or agent can make the same edit.
sheet.getRange('B2').setValue(4)

univerAPI.getFormula().onCalculationResultApplied().then(() => {
  console.log(sheet.getRange('D4').getValue()) // 200
  localStorage.setItem('quotation', JSON.stringify(workbook.save()))
}).catch(console.error)

The editor and your application operate on the same workbook; formula changes are recalculated automatically. returns a JSON snapshot containing the workbook and its registered plugin data. Your application owns persistence; this example uses browser storage. On a later page load, after initialization, restore the snapshot instead of creating a blank workbook:

const saved = localStorage.getItem('quotation')
if (saved) {
  univerAPI.createWorkbook(JSON.parse(saved))
}

This workflow uses only open-source packages. Snapshot persistence is separate from XLSX import and export, which uses the separately distributed file-conversion capabilities. Use public Facade APIs for application integration; the source links below explain internal implementation and extension points. See the API Stability Policy before depending on an extension point.

🏗️ Explore the open-source architecture

Give custom features clear boundaries

Univer organizes content logic and UI interaction in separate plugins. Feature plugins manage rules and content changes; UI plugins provide the interface and user interactions. For example, manages filter ranges and rules, while provides panels, menus, and shortcuts.

%%{init: {'htmlLabels': false, 'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Arial, PingFang SC, Microsoft YaHei, sans-serif', 'fontSize': '17px', 'lineColor': '#64748b'}, 'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': false, 'curve': 'linear', 'nodeSpacing': 28, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'padding': 16, 'wrappingWidth': 270}}}%%
%% A layered overview, not a complete dependency graph.
%% Group arrows indicate reuse of the layer below; internal arrows show selected dependencies.
flowchart TD
  subgraph FEATURES["Feature Plugins"]
    direction LR
    FUI["Filter<br/>UI Plugin"]
    VUI["Data Validation<br/>UI Plugin"]
    FILTER["Filter Plugin"]
    VALIDATION["Data Validation Plugin"]
    FUI --> FILTER
    VUI --> VALIDATION
  end

  subgraph PRODUCTS["Product Plugins"]
    direction LR
    SUI["Sheets UI Plugin"]
    SHEETS["Sheets Plugin"]
    SUI --> SHEETS
  end

  subgraph FOUNDATION["Core Framework & Plugins"]
    direction LR
    UI["UI Plugin"]
    FORMULA["Formula Engine Plugin"]
    RENDER["Render Engine Plugin"]
    CORE["Core"]
    UI --> RENDER
    RENDER --> CORE
    FORMULA --> CORE
  end

  FEATURES --> PRODUCTS
  PRODUCTS --> FOUNDATION

  classDef logic fill:#eff6ff,color:#17365f,stroke:#93b4df,stroke-width:1.5px
  classDef ui fill:#f0fdf4,color:#17543a,stroke:#91c8a7,stroke-width:1.5px
  classDef shared fill:#f6f7f9,color:#334155,stroke:#bac3ce,stroke-width:1.5px
  classDef feature fill:#172d50,color:#ffffff,stroke:#172d50
  class FUI,VUI ui
  class FILTER,VALIDATION logic
  class SUI,SHEETS logic
  class UI,FORMULA,RENDER,CORE shared

  style FEATURES fill:#f7fcf9,stroke:#b5d8c1,color:#17543a
  style PRODUCTS fill:#f5f9ff,stroke:#b6cbea,color:#17365f
  style FOUNDATION fill:#fafbfc,stroke:#cbd2dc,color:#334155

Figure 1: three plugin layers. Feature plugins build on product plugins, which reuse the core framework and plugins. Group arrows show dependencies on the layer below; Core provides content models, commands, dependency injection, and lifecycle management. Some plugins and dependencies are omitted.

New features keep their rules in their own plugins and cooperate through public services, commands, and defined extension points. UI plugins build on shared UI services and components.

Dependencies are explicit at two levels:

  • declares runtime plugin dependencies. The plugin service orders them, and lifecycle stages separate dependency registration, content initialization, and UI initialization.
  • dependency injection connects controllers and services through declared dependencies. Supported overrides let an application replace an implementation, adapt a platform service, or supply a test double. Instance-scoped injectors keep application state separate between Univer instances.

Disposable registration also gives commands, listeners, components, and icons a cleanup path when their owner is disposed.

Compose cross-feature edits and undo/redo

For example, when rows are inserted inside a filter range, the filter plugin supplies the corresponding range change and its undo data. The row command composes the base edit and participating feature changes, executes them, and records their undo/redo information together. The row insertion feature can use the shared extension mechanism while the filter plugin owns its range-update rules.

The command system distinguishes three kinds of action:

  • orchestrates a business action and the changes it requires.
  • changes content saved in a snapshot, with serializable parameters.
  • changes transient state, such as an open panel or the scroll position.

A shared structure for undo/redo. For an undoable edit, the feature implementation supplies the forward mutations and corresponding inverse mutations, and the Command records them through . When one action affects several features, the Command can combine their changes and undo data in a single undo/redo record, so the user can undo and redo the complete action. See extending commands.

Features still need to cooperate. Interceptors and reference-range handlers give that cooperation a defined place. At supported extension points, plugins contribute checks or related mutations; interceptor priorities control ordering where the API defines it.

These boundaries support a practical testing strategy: test models and services independently, replace external dependencies through DI, and add regression cases for combined actions and undo/redo. The filter controller tests exercise row and column changes and their effect on filtering.

Connect applications and agents through Facade APIs and events

The repository includes the content models, formula engine, and Canvas rendering and layout engine behind the editors. They are shared building blocks: spreadsheet rich text, for example, reuses document layout and rendering. Custom features can build on these engines instead of implementing a separate content stack. Read about the formula engine architecture and rendering engine architecture.

Browser editors, Node.js Headless tasks, and appropriately composed Workers can reuse the corresponding content plugins, models, commands, and calculation. See Headless Univer and the isomorphic architecture.

exposes execution callbacks so plugins can observe commands before and after execution. Facade APIs wrap the underlying capabilities in application objects such as , , and .

Each plugin contributes its own Facade extensions, typed events through , and enums through . Application code can discover event names and constants from one entry point instead of importing private services or repeating strings. For example, can inspect and cancel an execution; reports executions to listeners. Listeners return disposables, and cancellation applies where the event supports it.

🧩 Extend your application with Univer Office SDK

When you want more ready-to-integrate capabilities, compose the corresponding modules: additional content types, advanced editing plugins, collaboration, file conversion, and agent tooling. They extend the same content models, plugin architecture, command system, and Facade design introduced above, so you can build on your existing integration.

How it extends the foundation
Open-source Web SDK core · this repositoryOpen-source models, engines, plugins, UI foundation, and Sheets and Docs capabilities, with corresponding Headless content operations. Use them in commercial applications under Apache-2.0.
Commercial Web SDK pluginsFollow the core's Plugin, dependency injection, Command/Mutation, and Facade extension patterns. Add charts, shapes, pivot tables, SmartArt, and other features for the corresponding content types.
Extends the same content models and mutation conventions with real-time collaboration, revision history, and Office file conversion. Integrates with your application's identity, permissions, and storage.
Reuse Web SDK Headless and Facade capabilities to provide composable Node.js APIs and CLI building blocks for agents to inspect, edit, and check content, with collaboration and Worktree review integrations.
  • Apache-2.0 packages that can be used in commercial applications under that license, including the open-source Headless content capabilities.
  • Commercial Web SDK plugins, Server SDK, and AI SDK capabilities beyond the open-source foundation are distributed and licensed separately. evaluation includes watermarks and feature limits.
  • Open-source applications such as Univer Workspace have their own source licenses. Their SDK dependencies retain their respective licenses.

🌐 Application patterns and ecosystem

Univer Workspace: an Office SDK reference application

For a complete application reference, start with Univer Workspace. It shows how to compose Univer Office SDK editors, collaboration, file capabilities, existing agents, and human review into a self-hostable workspace. Follow its integration patterns when building your own Office application or agent workspace.

Workspace is open source; its SDK dependencies follow their respective licenses. See the Workspace overview for connected apps and review workflows.

CLI, agent integrations, and developer skills

The same SDK capabilities can also be composed into the agents and tools you already use:

Each repository documents its setup and SDK dependencies. Explore the ecosystem for agent entry points, or the documentation to build your own integration.

📚 Documentation and contributing

Thanks to all contributors who build and improve Univer. Contributions to engines, plugins, tests, documentation, and examples are welcome.

Univer is compiled with a Chrome 88 target and aims to work with the versions listed above.

  • : Univer relies on . Add a polyfill such as if your target browser or runtime does not provide it.
  • : We recommend Vite, esbuild, or Webpack 5. If your build tool does not support the field in (common in Webpack 4), you may need extra path mapping.
  • : Univer's view layer is built on React 18, supports React 18 and 19, and provides minimal compatibility support for React 16.9+ and 17.
  • : Headless Univer supports Node.js . Developing this monorepo requires Node.js .

If you believe you have found a security issue, please follow the Security Policy.

Univer is supported by the community and sponsors. You can support the project through Open Collective.

Copyright (c) 2021-present DreamNum Co., Ltd.

The open-source packages in this repository are licensed under Apache-2.0. Commercial SDK modules are distributed and licensed separately.

items.title: ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp
items.content:
Chrome DevTools for coding agents

Chrome DevTools for agents () lets your coding agent (such as Antigravity, Claude, Cursor or Copilot) control and inspect a live Chrome browser. It is available as a Model-Context-Protocol (MCP) server and as a CLI. Both give your AI coding assistant access to the full power of Chrome DevTools for reliable automation, in-depth debugging, and performance analysis.

  • : Uses Chrome DevTools to record traces and extract actionable performance insights.
  • Advanced browser debugging: Analyze network requests, take screenshots and check browser console messages (with source-mapped stack traces).
  • . Uses puppeteer to automate actions in Chrome and automatically wait for action results.

exposes content of the browser instance to the MCP clients allowing them to inspect, debug, and modify any data in the browser or DevTools. Avoid sharing sensitive or personal information that you don't want to share with MCP clients.

officially supports Google Chrome and Chrome for Testing only. Other Chromium-based browsers may work, but this is not guaranteed, and you may encounter unexpected behavior. Use at your own discretion. We are committed to providing fixes and support for the latest version of Extended Stable Chrome.

Performance tools may send trace URLs to the Google CrUX API to fetch real-user experience data. This helps provide a holistic performance picture by presenting field data alongside lab data. This data is collected by the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX). To disable this, run with the flag.

Google collects usage statistics (such as tool invocation success rates, latency, and environment information) to improve the reliability and performance of Chrome DevTools MCP.

Data collection is . You can opt-out by passing the flag when starting the server:

"args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest", "--no-usage-statistics"]

Google's collection of usage statistics for Chrome DevTools MCP is independent from the Chrome browser's usage statistics. Opting out of Chrome metrics does not automatically opt you out of this tool, and vice-versa.

Collection is disabled if CHROME_DEVTOOLS_MCP_NO_USAGE_STATISTICS or env variables are set.

By default, the server periodically checks the npm registry for updates and logs a notification when a newer version is available. You can disable these update checks by setting the CHROME_DEVTOOLS_MCP_NO_UPDATE_CHECKS environment variable.

Add the following config to your MCP client:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "chrome-devtools": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"]
    }
  }
}

Using chrome-devtools-mcp@latest ensures that your MCP client will always use the latest version of the Chrome DevTools MCP server.

For setup instructions specific to your editor or agent (e.g. Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code), please see our Client Configurations Guide.

Enter the following prompt in your MCP Client to check if everything is working:

Check the performance of https://developers.chrome.com

Your MCP client should open the browser and record a performance trace.

The MCP server will start the browser automatically once the MCP client uses a tool that requires a running browser instance. Connecting to the Chrome DevTools MCP server on its own will not automatically start the browser.

The package also includes the CLI. Use it to control the browser from your terminal without MCP:

npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
chrome-devtools navigate_page 1 --url "https://developers.chrome.com"
chrome-devtools take_screenshot 1 --filePath screenshot.png
chrome-devtools stop

See the CLI guide for all commands and options.

The package includes skills that teach your agent how to use Chrome DevTools:

Install skills as a plugin

A plugin installs the MCP server and all skills, including the CLI skill:

  • Run /plugin marketplace add ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp, then /plugin install chrome-devtools-mcp@chrome-devtools-plugins.
  • Run Chat: Install Plugin From Source and enter ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp.
  • Run gemini extensions install --auto-update https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp.

If your agent does not support plugins, copy the skill folders into the skills directory of your agent. The npm package contains the skills:

npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
# Example for Claude Code. Use the skills directory of your agent.
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -R "$(npm root -g)/chrome-devtools-mcp/skills/chrome-devtools-cli" ~/.claude/skills/

The skill requires the CLI. Install the package globally before you use the skill.

Skills describe the tools of a specific version. Update the skills each time you update the MCP server or the CLI. Outdated skills can tell your agent to use tools or parameters that changed.

  • Use the update command of the plugin manager of your agent. The Gemini CLI command above enables automatic updates with .
  • Update the package, then copy the skill folders again:
npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -R "$(npm root -g)/chrome-devtools-mcp/skills/chrome-devtools-cli" ~/.claude/skills/

Find the complete list of server parameters (e.g., , , ) and how to configure WebSocket connections in the Configuration Guide.

For basic browser tasks only, the flag exposes a reduced set of tools. See the Slim tool reference.

For advanced features such as handling concurrent sessions, persistent user data directories, using a custom or non-standard browser path (), connecting to a running Chrome instance instead of starting a new one, or debugging on Android, see our Advanced Usage Guide.

Integrating as a browser subagent

If you are developing agentic tooling and want to provide an integrated browser subagent as part of your product, we recommend building on top of Chrome DevTools for agents.

items.title: Likely7/Veyra-NRVideo
items.content:
Bring PS5 GTA6 to 120FPS with DLSS 5. An advanced Windows video player and capture enhancement tool featuring real-time preview for videos, images, and capture card sources. Combine AI-powered Super Resolution, DLSS5 image enhancement, and Frame Generation to deliver a next-generation visual experience.

One engine. Any source. Real-time enhancement.

Open source · GPL-3.0 · Windows 11 · C++ · DirectX 12 · NVIDIA & AMD

dual SR, SR-then-downsample, NVIDIA Low Latency, experimental RX 7000 NR and capture/FG/audio/volume fixes. Full update and migration.

2.1.1 historical release, 2026-10-27: processed-picture recording with audio,90° playback rotation, per-layer NR percentage controls and export sizing, event-driven refresh/VRR/HDR queries, AMD HDR+NR handling, AA ordering, capture timestamp handling, NR shutdown, popup layout, screenshots and fullscreen fixes. All changes since2.1.0.

New-effect cost examples: RTX5070 standard4K anti-aliasing fixtures: FXAA~0.15ms, SMAA/MLAA~0.30ms. Final single-face mesh beauty:1080p~0.93ms,4K~1.42ms. Costs vary with content/hardware; no local AMD speedup percentage was measured. Conditions and limits.

Instant replay/F9, microphone mixing/separate tracks, all-effect exclusion, VFR dedup/60→30 and presentation/logging repairs, refined flow, updated defaults and collapsed HDR controls. All changes and measured data. ANR host source is included; its runtime is not distributed.

Smoother frame pacing after capture deduplication and preview correction for invalid capture timestamps. Full changes.

Optional VB-CABLE capture audio, DLSS/FSR/RTX dual super resolution, NVIDIA DLAA, HDR wide-gamut restoration, NR inference reuse, 1% low FPS, and recording and compatibility fixes. Full changes and settings migration.

Three RTX Video SR families and independent second-pass models, medium defaults, inline NR web/list editing, RTX30 VFG compatibility, RX7000 multi-GPU and seeking/menu fixes. Full changes, comparison and migration.

each NR layer's Enhancement delta → Total strength now reaches 5. defaults off; enable it and select Automatic or Manual. Automatic values now adapt separately to styles 0/1/2, with an amount slider (0 retains raw strength, 1 applies full correction). The nine manual controls cover hue, chroma, neutral tint, source color retention, lightness retention, shadows, highlights, local compression and temporal stability. Use this style’s automatic values provides a manual starting point. Switching modes keeps manual values; turning control off preserves the original residual algorithm. Five extrapolates one inference's residual, and protection reduces the corresponding changes; it cannot promise full gain five with no artifacts on every video. Presets, List/Node sessions, PNGs and video exports share the settings. Local validation and known limits.

  • Home, Cinema, Professional List, Nodes, Colour, Export and Settings; Simplified/Traditional Chinese, English and Japanese.
  • Node editing and layered NR: executable connections, independent NR/colour parameters, separate List/Node configurations, sessions and presets.
  • Moonlight/Sunshine-compatible PC streaming and unofficial experimental Xbox support, alongside PS5, capture cards and screen capture.
  • editable ordered queue, trimming, MP4/MKV, multiple audio/embedded subtitle tracks, cancellation/retry and completion sound.
  • Enhancement and compatibility: SF310.9.16 performance/legacy models, NVIDIA original for RTX50 and AMD lmxxf, DLSS/XeSS/FSR options, capture improvements and a persistent OBS Game Capture switch with restart confirmation. Full details are in the Release.
  • true dual RTX Video SR with separate second-pass controls, plus SR-then-downsample; ordinary 8K retained, new graphs check VRAM budget.
  • NVIDIA Low Latency Off / On / On + Boost; experimental RX 7000 RedDuke NR, Small/Original and per-layer scale; separate RX 9000 path retained.
  • sparse-noise-tolerant full-frame dedup, remove coarse generated-frame discard, smoothed anchors, optional VFG regulation, adaptive VSync capacity wait capped at 3 ms.
  • WGC high-refresh cadence, ready-immediate no-FG capture, first-copy 60→30, Dolby/DTS carriers on generic PCM pins.
  • F7 screenshot / F8 recording in game mode too; Cinema volume dragging, endpoints, Enter/click-away confirmation and focus.

  • Interface and SR defaults: software UI drawing by default, an optional GPU renderer with restart confirmation, and RTX Video SR high as the new SR model selection; saved model choices are retained.

  • record the processed picture with player audio; rotate playback90° in Cinema/Professional with matching preview and window layout.

  • per-layer25–100% scale controls, saved presets/sessions and fixed/percentage video-export inference sizes with independent output resolution.

  • Display and frame generation: background event-driven refresh/VRR/HDR queries, shared signal-panel refresh and HDR-cache recovery.

  • correct AMD FSR-off state, native-HDR NR proxy/reconstruction and List-mode AA placement after NR.

  • Interaction and lifecycle: popup first-open layout, real screenshot paths/formats, fullscreen/maximized restoration, playlist key ownership, capture preparation timestamps and NR/NVAPI teardown.

  • RX9000 Small/Original models via the per-layer performance switch(default on), saved in presets/sessions/export; explicit asset errors, no new RX6000/7000 support.
  • independent FXAA/SMAA/MLAA, List/Nodes, quality/strength controls, HDR and List export; experimental temporal SMAA defaults off.
  • Beauty and original-face restoration: separate switches, up to six layers,468-point contours, eye/brow/lip exclusion, per-frame detection and smoothing; restoration mixes the pre-effect source back into faces.
  • native enumeration fallback, driver ranges/steps/custom-size checks, searchable legacy list, exact rate/pixel-format matching, explicit substitution rejection, saved/resumed capture settings.
  • Network and AVerMedia audio: shared buffering/reconnect, slow-server buffering status, HLS/interlaced damage handling, throttled subtitle scanning; vendor multichannel audio, non-PCM confirmation, complete-payload decode and bounded recovery.
  • game-mode handoff/hotkeys/scaling/static resize, fullscreen transport/cursor, disabled-node order and export protocol consistency, home/sponsor page, corrected Bilibili profile and complete new translations.

Download Veyra-2.1.6-NVIDIA-win64-portable.zip or Veyra-2.1.6-AMD-win64-portable.zip for Veyra's active GPU. Extract with Windows or 7-Zip into a new writable folder and run . You need one GPU package to run the application; source assets are only for rebuilding. Windows 11 x64 and DirectX 12 are required; Qt and approved runtimes are included, while GPU/capture drivers are installed separately. Backend hardware requirements vary; most local tests used an RTX 5070.

Start with effects off, check picture/sound, then enable effects individually. High resolution, layered NR and frame generation increase GPU/VRAM requirements.

The 1.4.4 UI guide is obsolete. Version 2.0 uses separate settings. Retain the old version for rollback; do not overwrite the new package with old , an entire folder or mixed DLLs.

prefer extracting into a new folder; copy only runtime_local/user-data-2.0.0 and custom after closing Veyra. Use Settings→About for custom paths. Same-flavour in-place overlay is possible after exit but leaves stale components. Steps.

Historical 2.1.0→2.1.1 migration: close Veyra and back up user data first. Overlay the matching GPU package contents into the existing executable directory to retain its data folder. For a new installation directory on the same PC, open Settings→About→User data in the old version, then close it and copy its folder into the new package’s directory. Copy only the data folder to keep the new runtime files; custom data-directory launches use the location shown in the app.

Home offers files, capture card, PS5, PC, Xbox and screen capture. Files/images can also be dropped into the window. Move to the bottom edge to reveal navigation between Home, Cinema, Professional, Colour, Export and Settings.

  • Cinema prioritises the picture with a floating source/transport/audio/fullscreen bar, optionally hidden in settings.
  • Professional List has Picture, Frame generation, Colour, Sound and Display tabs. The order strip locates effects; bottom panels report source/output, GPU stage time and load.
  • Click a file's picture to pause/resume; left/right arrows seek five seconds. Double-click or use the fullscreen button. The fullscreen top-edge bar switches Cinema/Professional; opens quick controls in fullscreen List mode, locks controls. Shortcuts are configurable.
  • Use Screenshot and the preset menu to save pictures and personal settings. No imposed built-in quality presets.

The NR version selector offers RTX20–50 · SF310.9.16, RTX50 · NVIDIA original and RX 7000 / 9000 · AMD NR (experimental; routed to RedDuke/lmxxf by GPU) in both List and Node mode. SF defaults to performance modelB; disable Use performance model for legacyA. The control is disabled for NVIDIA original; AMD0.44 selects Small when enabled(default) and Original when disabled. Model selection is saved per layer. Lecram/oldSF-v2 settings migrate to SF. Unsupported versions remain visible but gray; switching supported versions updates the entire NR chain. AMD NR requires driver HIP 7. Video export uses at most internal 1080p inference and composites to the original output size; this is not native 4K NR and image exports retain the native model pixel budget. Version2.1.1 processes AMD native-HDR NR through an SDR-linear proxy and reconstructs the result over the HDR base (2.1.1 details). See current runtime identities.

Select List at the top of Professional. Enable SR, NR or RTX Video HDR as needed. Up to four NR layers have independent internal resolution, strength and parameters. The master switch disables all layers and restores their previous enabled states.

List mode's global NR protection region excludes every NR layer inside it while retaining non-NR effects, useful for HUDs/subtitles. Colour controls include basic adjustments, curves, mixer, wheels, LUTs and colour presets.

Choose a supported FG backend/multiplier and check cadence, display sync, low-queue mode and output cap. Original/enhanced comparison temporarily pauses FG; leaving it resumes FG. Submitted FPS is not physical display FPS or end-to-end latency.

Node mode — build a processing chain

Select Nodes at the top of Professional. This is an executable chain editor:

  1. Keep a valid connected path from input to output. Right-click blank canvas or choose Add node.
  2. Drag an output port to an input port, or click the two ports in order. Drop a node on a wire to insert; drag it away or release with held to disconnect.
  3. Edit parameters inside nodes. NR/colour nodes have independent settings and supported positions before/after SR. Right-click to delete, duplicate or reset. A duplicate is an independent until connected.
  4. Middle-drag to pan, wheel to zoom. Fit/auto-layout organise the graph. “Draft not running” means invalid/disconnected edits, not that every visible node executes.
  5. Optical flow is shared after input; SR is a single instance. RTX Video HDR stays before final FG; select one DLSS/XeSS/FSR backend. This is not an arbitrary branching/mixing graph.
  6. List and Node settings, presets and sessions are separate. Returning to List restores its settings and retains the node graph. Switching rebuilds processing and may briefly pause the picture.

2.0.8 Node mode does not support offline export or List mode's global NR protection region. Switch to List and verify its effects before exporting; graphs are not silently converted.

Select device, resolution, rate, then a supported pixel format and audio input. Close competing apps. Match PQ/HLG/709 and Limited/Full to the signal. Magewell Pro Capture has a dedicated low-latency option.
Enable Remote Play and discover/enter the console IP. Click to open PSNTools, copy the numeric or Base64 Account ID back into Veyra, then enter the console’s eight-digit pairing code. Saved consoles reconnect directly.
Install/configure Sunshine yourself; discover/add the host, PIN-pair, select app/desktop and connect. Sunshine is not bundled.
Follow device-code sign-in and select a console with remote features enabled. Unofficial/experimental; account, service and console restrictions apply.
Select a window/display; avoid recursively capturing Veyra itself.

For Screen Capture → Game mode, choose a borderless game window or monitor. opens adjustments, Home/Esc closes them, exits passthrough. For Capture card → PS5 controller control, pair the console first; third-party streaming software can relay this PC's enhanced picture and forward remote input. Enable background controller forwarding and audio monitoring as needed. See the2.0.8 update for setup and hardware limits. Hotkeys are now customizable in Settings → Shortcuts; defaults stay Home/Ctrl+Alt+Home. Windowed game pictures follow the original visible bounds; use borderless fullscreen to fill the display.

Pausing capture/streaming freezes the preview while keeping the session, not the host game. Physical hardware, networks, HDR and controllers need individual validation.

Use , confirm effects, then open Export. Add/reorder files, edit individual jobs, trim, select MP4/MKV and encoding quality, and keep all or selected audio/subtitle tracks.

Keep all skips unsupported tracks with a notice; explicitly choosing an incompatible track is an error. Pause/cancel/retry and completion sound are available. Defaults are VBR 8 Mbps and closing playback on export to free GPU resources, both adjustable. Live FG does not imply every backend supports offline FG; follow accepted export settings.

For OBS Game Capture, enable Settings → General & appearance → OBS Game Capture compatibility. Saved immediately: Yes restarts now; No applies next launch. Finish exports before restarting. Software UI rendering simplifies some shadows/blur; video enhancement stays on GPU. Game Capture targets ; use Windows 10 (1903+) Window Capture for the whole UI.

Settings → General & appearance → Resume last source at startup is opt-in. It restores the movie position or saved capture device, format, rate and audio selection. Startup page is configurable. Use the playback-speed button in Cinema or Professional for 1× / 1.5× / 2× / 3×; this does not speed up live capture/streams or offline exports.

defaults to Auto: when RTSS (MSI Afterburner OSD) is running at launch, the interface uses software rendering and its OSD appears on the video only. If RTSS starts later, restart Veyra when prompted. Using RTSS with OBS Game Capture requires RTSS’s “Use Microsoft Detours API hooking” option for Veyra, or use OBS Window Capture.

select a compute GPU, optionally enable RTX50 DLSS performance mode or variable refresh, and check update status. Startup checks show a temporary banner only for a newer release. Douyin Live Companion detection uses a software interface at launch and temporarily caps requested realtime GPU priority at High while it is running, restoring the requested value afterwards.

Settings include language/scale, shortcuts, monitoring GPU, audio devices and component info. Report GPU/driver, media, effects, time and ; include a crash if available. Review private data before sharing.

RTSS compatibility was verified locally with RTSS 7.3.7 on an RTX 5070; GamePP and other overlay/hardware combinations remain unverified. Real-console Xbox long runs and console/VRR capture still need field retesting. RTX 30/40 community NR/FG, FSR 4 ML hardware, some NR TDR/VRAM-growth reports and cross-device streaming retain unresolved/unverified cases. See the Release. Community runtimes are not vendor certification or a complete official DLSS 5 integration.

flowchart TD
    UI[Qt Quick / QML pages] --> Bridge[Shared Bridge / settings / sessions / presets]
    Sources[Files / capture / PS5 / PC / Xbox / screen] --> Source[FrameSource: frames, timestamps, colour]
    Bridge --> Graph[Shared EnhanceGraph: valid chain]
    Source --> Graph
    Graph --> Effects[Multiple NR / single SR / colour / Video HDR]
    Effects --> Live[Live preview: optional final FG]
    Live --> Present[Native D3D12 video window]
    Effects --> Export[List offline export / screenshots]
    Export --> Sink[Encoding and muxing / image files]
    Bridge --> Queue[Export queue: per-job settings snapshot]
    Queue --> Export

QML renders UI; native D3D12 renders video. List/Nodes share the engine, disconnected drafts do not execute, and export does not record the preview window.

2.1.6 integrates the presentation/capture/low-latency, cadence and UI repairs; see the full update and measurement limits. The independently written ANR host is traceable in source. No ANR DLLs, models or program packs are distributed because upstream explicitly prohibits third-party redistribution during the beta.

Original code: GPL-3.0. The combined Chiaki streaming application is also subject to AGPL-3.0 and its OpenSSL exception (licenses/remoteplay). Third-party notices, 2.1.2 build/source. Source Git excludes proprietary runtimes/models. Release manifests audit publisher files, not hash-lock user DLL replacements.

items.title: tailscale/tailcat
items.content:
like netcat, but over Tailscale's data plane, without Tailscale's control plane

"Tailscale without Tailscale, by Tailscale"

Tailcat is a remix of Tailscale open source pieces to act like netcat, but over Tailscale's data plane, without Tailscale's control plane. Tailscale's data plane (, internally) gives you point-to-point WireGuard®-encrypted tunnels between two machines with DERP as the NAT-hole-punching communication side channel and the ultimate relay-of-last-resort if NAT traversal fails. Instead of using the Tailscale control plane, all connection metadata is exchanged out of band, however you want.

Whether you use as a CLI tool or library, one side runs a server (listener) and gets back a short tailcat address. The other side passes that tailcat address to 's client side to connect. All traffic between the two is encrypted end-to-end with WireGuard. The initial connection bootstraps through a DERP server (see below), and then magicsock performs NAT traversal to upgrade to a direct peer-to-peer UDP connection when possible (usually!).

You don't need a Tailscale account, root/admin access on the machine (it doesn't alter your machine's routing tables, DNS, etc.). It's just a userspace library and CLI tool.

And it's all open source.

There's also an experimental in-browser web demo (tailcat compiled to WebAssembly) at https://tailscale.github.io/tailcat/ that can send and receive files or text, interoperating with the CLI. Browser traffic is relayed over DERP only, with no direct connections until WebRTC support (#4).

See INSTALL.md for details on each, including notes for packagers building from source:

Pipe stdin/stdout between two machines

Server starts, printing out its ephemeral address:

$ tailcat
# Selected bootstrap relay region 302, San Francisco
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcomFwWCCcjS5nKNqAod034nWoJZW0LZqDhhC8U_dKdnDRYQ8uNGFpGQEu
(hangs, waiting...)

$ echo hello | tailcat tcomFwWCCcjS5nKNqAod034nWoJZW0LZqDhhC8U_dKdnDRYQ8uNGFpGQEu
$

Then the server unblocks:

$ tailcat
# Selected bootstrap relay region 302, San Francisco
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcomFwWCCcjS5nKNqAod034nWoJZW0LZqDhhC8U_dKdnDRYQ8uNGFpGQEu
hello
$

Expose local ports through the tunnel

Or you can serve a local TCP port, forwarded to localhost:

$ tailcat serve 8080,8443 # or: tailcat serve all
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX

$ tailcat tcXXXXXXXXX 8080
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: foo

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
....

A port mapping proxies a port somewhere other than the same port on localhost: to a different local port, or to a host and port elsewhere on the server's network. This serves port 5555 by proxying it to an Android device's adb port on the LAN, without exposing the rest of the network the way would:

$ tailcat serve 5555:10.2.200.213:5555
# Proxying port 5555 to 10.2.200.213:5555
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX

Then on the client, tailcat forward tcXXXXXXXXX 5555 followed by adb connect 127.0.0.1:5555. Write IPv6 targets in brackets: .

Forward local ports to a tailcat server

To make ports served by a tailcat server available as ordinary local TCP ports (for browsers, database clients, or other tools that do not support SOCKS or stdio), run with the server's tailcat address:

$ tailcat serve 8080,3306
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX

$ tailcat forward tcXXXXXXXXX 18080:8080 3306

A local port of 0 asks the operating system for a free port; each listener prints its address once it's listening.

To forward local ports to assets on the network reachable by an exit-node server, run the server in exit-node mode and specify each remote IP address and port in the mapping:

$ tailcat serve exit-node
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX

$ tailcat forward tcXXXXXXXXX \
    3001:172.23.52.30:3001 \
    17170:172.23.52.31:17170

This forwards to and to through the exit-node server.

By default, listeners bind to and diagnostic logs are suppressed. Pass before the subcommand to enable verbose networking logs. Use only when clients on other machines should be able to connect:

$ tailcat forward --bind=0.0.0.0 tcXXXXXXXXX 18080:8080

Press Ctrl-C to stop forwarding.

Open a browser to a tailcat server

To view a web server behind a tailcat server, run :

$ tailcat serve 80
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX

$ tailcat browse tcXXXXXXXXX

This is an alias for tailcat forward --open-browser <tc-addr> 0:80: it opens in a web browser once the local listener is ready, then blocks, forwarding connections, until interrupted. The flag works with any single port mapping.

Public-key-authenticated SSH server

Run an SSH server that accepts keys from local files, literal OpenSSH public key lines, or GitHub accounts:

$ tailcat serve --ssh-authorized-keys=~/.ssh/authorized_keys ssh
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX

Multiple sources can be comma-separated. A source fetches https://github.com/user.keys once, before the server starts:

$ tailcat serve --ssh-authorized-keys=bradfitz@github,./contractor.pub ssh

Every source must exist, fetch successfully, and contain valid public key lines or startup fails. Authorized-key options such as and are rejected because the built-in server does not implement them. Running without also fails; use the explicit service when the tunnel identity alone is sufficient.

On Linux, macOS, and Windows, you can also explicitly run the SSH server with no client authentication. The encrypted tunnel provides the client identity.

$ tailcat serve no-auth-ssh
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX

With , the address the credential: anyone who learns it gets a shell as the user running the server. Share it only over private channels, and never publish it, in a DNS TXT record or anywhere else public. If you want an SSH server reachable by DNS name, it must require client authentication: at the tunnel layer, at the SSH layer, or both.

$ tailcat ssh tcXXXXXXXXX
$ tailcat ssh tcXXXXXXXXX ls -la

Run a command per connection

Like inetd, the service runs a command for each incoming connection, with the connection as the command's stdin and stdout. The command comes after :

$ tailcat serve exec -- /usr/bin/fortune
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX

$ tailcat tcXXXXXXXXX 80 < /dev/null

The command's stderr goes to the server's. It gets the peer's node key in (in 's format) and the peer's tailcat IP:port in .

Given with the or service, the command instead replaces the shell, like OpenSSH's : every SSH session runs only that command (on a PTY if the client asks for one), and the server offers no shell, no client-chosen command, and no SFTP. The client's requested command, if any, arrives in .

$ tailcat serve --ssh-authorized-keys=alice@github ssh -- ./deploy.sh
$ tailcat serve no-auth-ssh -- git-upload-pack /srv/repo.git

To receive files, run a drop box and share the printed tailcat address:

$ tailcat recv ~/inbox
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX

$ tailcat cp report.pdf tcXXXXXXXXX:

runs the system with the connection routed through tailcat, so you get its usual progress display, and for directory trees. The drop box is write-only: senders can't list the directory, read anything back, or touch existing files.

To offer files instead, serve a directory read-only (the default) or read-write:

$ tailcat serve files                  # current directory, read-only
$ tailcat serve --files=/pub:rw files  # a given directory, read-write

$ tailcat ls -l tcXXXXXXXXX
$ tailcat cp tcXXXXXXXXX:report.pdf .

speaks SFTP natively, so it works even without OpenSSH installed.

The server confines all paths to the served directory (via Go's ), so neither nor symlinks escape it. The file service speaks SFTP, so the stock and clients also work against it, given a ProxyCommand that pipes through tailcat (the same trick and use). Both and servers serve SFTP too, with the same access as the shell.

Transfers are not compressed: the SFTP protocol has no compression of its own, and the SSH transport here doesn't either (Go's SSH stack omits it; transport compression has a history of security problems, and TLS dropped it too). Compress files before sending if it matters.

Measure throughput and latency

Run an iperf-like test between two machines. The server accepts tests with the service and the client sends to it for 10 seconds by default, printing progress each second and both sides' totals at the end. sends the other way, both ways at once, tests UDP (paced to , default 1 Mbit/s) and reports loss, reordering, and jitter, and runs several streams. Round trips over the test's control connection measure latency while the tunnel is loaded:

$ tailcat serve perf
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX

$ tailcat perf tcXXXXXXXXX
# path: direct via 203.0.113.7:41641, rtt 1.2ms
TCP, client -> server, 1 stream, 10s
[   1.0s]  sent    118 MB    943 Mbit/s  rtt 2.1ms
...
sent        1.18 GB in   10.0s    943 Mbit/s
received    1.18 GB in   10.0s    942 Mbit/s
rtt under load  min 1.9ms  avg 2.3ms  max 4.1ms  (50 samples)

The test first waits for a direct path (up to ) and refuses to run through a DERP relay otherwise, since a throughput test through a shared relay mostly measures its rate limit while crowding out everyone else. allows a relayed test through a relay you run yourself; Tailscale's shared relays are always refused. prints the results as JSON.

Ping to test connectivity; each pong reports whether it arrived via a DERP relay or a direct path. keeps pinging (up to , default 10s) until a direct path works, exiting non-zero if one doesn't:

$ tailcat ping --until-direct <tc-addr>
pong in 42.1ms via DERP(sfo)
pong in 1.2ms via 203.0.113.7:41641

Run a command through a SOCKS5 proxy routed over the tunnel:

$ tailcat socks <tc-addr> curl http://server.tailcat:8081/

Tailcat addresses also work directly as URL hostnames: the SOCKS proxy recognizes and dials them, so the tailcat address argument is optional. (Tailcat addresses are case-sensitive; this works with curl and most CLI tools, but not with browsers, which lowercase hostnames.)

$ tailcat socks curl http://<tc-addr>:8081/

Act as an exit node so the client can reach the server's network:

$ tailcat serve exit-node

Parse a tailcat address and print its contents (the server's WireGuard public key and DERP info) as JSON, without connecting to anything:

$ tailcat parse tcomFwWCCcjS5nKNqAod034nWoJZW0LZqDhhC8U_dKdnDRYQ8uNGFpGQEu
{
    "ServerPublic": "nodekey:9c8d2e6728da80a1dd37e275a82595b42d9a838610bc53f74a7670d1610f2e34",
    "RegionID": 302
}

Resolve a short tailcat address (which references a DERP region by ID, requiring clients to fetch the DERP map) into a longer self-contained one with the DERP server info embedded, letting clients connect more quickly:

$ tailcat resolve tcomFwWCCcjS5nKNqAod034nWoJZW0LZqDhhC8U_dKdnDRYQ8uNGFpGQEu
tcomFwWCCcjS5nKNqAod034nWoJZW0LZqDhhC8U_dKdnDRYQ8uNGFygaFhToGjYWhudGMzMDJhLmlwbi5kZXZhNG0yMDguMTExLjM5LjM4YTZzMjYwNzpmNzQwOjA6M2Y6OjcyMA

Parsing that resolved tailcat address shows the embedded DERP info:

$ tailcat parse tcomFwWCCcjS5nKNqAod034nWoJZW0LZqDhhC8U_dKdnDRYQ8uNGFygaFhToGjYWhudGMzMDJhLmlwbi5kZXZhNG0yMDguMTExLjM5LjM4YTZzMjYwNzpmNzQwOjA6M2Y6OjcyMA
{
    "ServerPublic": "nodekey:9c8d2e6728da80a1dd37e275a82595b42d9a838610bc53f74a7670d1610f2e34",
    "Region": [
        {
            "Nodes": [
                {
                    "HostName": "tc302a.ipn.dev",
                    "IPv4": "208.111.39.38",
                    "IPv6": "2607:f740:0:3f::720"
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}

A server can print the long self-contained form directly with the tailcat serve --full-address flag.

A server's tailcat address contains its WireGuard public key and an independent WireGuard pre-shared key, so the saved key material determines who can reach you:

  • Ephemeral keys (the default): each server run generates a fresh key in memory and prints an address nobody has ever seen. When the process exits, the key is discarded and the address is dead forever. This is the safe default: sharing that address only ever refers to that one run.

  • generates a key saved to disk so the address stays stable across restarts. The flip side: anyone you've shared that address with can connect to any future server using that key, unless you restrict clients with (see ).

The CLI says at startup which kind it's using, so you know whether you're starting a fresh single-use server or re-listening on an address you may have shared in the past.

WireGuard pre-shared keys are enabled by default and strongly recommended. For compatibility with tailcat clients v0.5.0 and earlier, on or produces shorter addresses, but removes post-quantum protection and protection from public DERP operators that observe the peers' public keys.

$ tailcat genkey --key=default --region=nyc
# prints the tailcat address; key saved to ~/.config/tailcat/keys/default.private.json

# later; the key named "default" is used automatically once it exists:
$ tailcat serve 8080
# 🐈 Server listening with saved key "default": tcXXXXXXXXX

# ... unless you force a one-off ephemeral key:
$ tailcat serve --key=new 8080
# 🐈 Server listening with new address: tcXXXXXXXXX

That is, is a magic key name: once it exists, plain silently uses it instead of generating an ephemeral key, and the startup line above is what tells you which happened. Use to get an ephemeral key anyway, to use a different saved key, or tailcat genkey --delete --key=default to remove the saved default key. lists your saved keys.

Tailcat addresses can also be published as DNS TXT records and looked up by name; a DNS name works anywhere the CLI takes a tailcat address:

# If example.com has a TXT record "tailcat=tc..."
$ tailcat example.com 8080
$ tailcat ssh example.com
$ tailcat ping example.com

A tailcat address is normally a secret: knowing it is what lets a client connect. A DNS TXT record is secret. It is public, world-readable, and actively scanned. Publishing an address in DNS hands it to everyone on the internet, so the server behind it must authenticate clients by something other than knowledge of the address: restrict the tunnel to known client keys with tailcat serve --allow=..., or, for SSH, require public keys with tailcat serve --ssh-authorized-keys=... ssh. Never publish the address of a server (or any other server that trusts whoever connects): that is a shell on your machine, published in a TXT record. See Protected SSH server over DNS for the safe setup.

Protected SSH server over DNS

Who needs port forwarding or port knocking? This runs an SSH server reachable from anywhere by name, with no open inbound ports on the server, where WireGuard authenticates the client before the SSH server ever sees a packet.

The flag below is not optional decoration. The DNS TXT record makes the tailcat address public, so possession of the address no longer proves anything: the server must authenticate clients itself, here by allowing only one client node key. Without (or SSH-level ), anyone on the internet who reads the TXT record can connect.

On the client machine, generate a client identity keypair. It prints the public key, which is all the server needs to know:

client$ tailcat genkey --client --key=client-default
# wrote file to ~/.config/tailcat/keys/client-default.private.json
nodekey:cfb6bfa77a0654d7450947fd6acef17d2cd848da1d30b2540b13dac272ddfd16

On the server, generate a server keypair pinned to its nearest DERP region (see why below), then serve SSH to only that client:

server$ tailcat genkey --key=default --fixed-region
# wrote file to ~/.config/tailcat/keys/default.private.json
tcXXXXXXXXX

server$ tailcat serve --allow=nodekey:cfb6bf...ddfd16 22
# 🐈 Server listening with saved key "default": tcXXXXXXXXX

Publish the tailcat address in DNS as a TXT record:

my-server.example.com. 300 IN TXT "tailcat=tcXXXXXXXXX"

And then the client side is just:

client$ tailcat ssh my-server.example.com

Client modes automatically use the saved key when it exists, so no extra flags are needed to present the allowed identity. Anyone else's handshake is silently ignored: they can't reach the SSH server, or even learn that one is running.

As a safety net, probes a DNS-named destination before connecting: it attempts an SSH login as a stranger would, with a freshly generated client key and no SSH credentials. If the server accepts that login, anyone who reads the TXT record could do the same, so tailcat refuses to connect and says why. The probe catches the misconfiguration the first time you test your own server; the flag skips it, whether because you really do want a public server or just to shave off the probe's round trips.

Why : it discovers the nearest DERP region once, at genkey time, and bakes its ID into both the printed tailcat address and the saved key file, so server restarts bind to the same region (keeping the published tailcat address valid) without re-probing. Otherwise genkey defaults to , which instead bakes in "pick at startup": fine for one-off use, but a tailcat address published in DNS should name a fixed region so clients and future server restarts all rendezvous in the same place. ( pins an explicit one instead; shows the choices.)

Bring your own DERP relay

Nothing requires Tailscale's relays: run your own DERP server (it needs a hostname with a TLS certificate, which derper can get itself via Let's Encrypt), then generate a server key that uses it by passing its hostname (or several, comma-separated) as the region:

server$ tailcat genkey --key=default --region=derp.example.com
tcomFwWCCAIsKOqPUux6ClG2RM4A_vOq4VBzGgHGGjq9OsJuFKSWFygaFhToGhYWhwZGVycC5leGFtcGxlLmNvbQ

server$ tailcat serve 22

The tailcat address embeds your relay's hostname:

$ tailcat parse tcomFwWCCAIsKOqPUux6ClG2RM4A_vOq4VBzGgHGGjq9OsJuFKSWFygaFhToGhYWhwZGVycC5leGFtcGxlLmNvbQ
{
    "ServerPublic": "nodekey:8022c28ea8f52ec7a0a51b644ce00fef3aae150731a01c61a3abd3ac26e14a49",
    "Region": [
        {
            "Nodes": [
                {
                    "HostName": "derp.example.com"
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}

so clients need no extra flags and never contact Tailscale's DERP map server or relays, and the only rate limits are yours. Alternatively, if you run a whole fleet of relays, serve your own DERP map JSON and point both sides at it with .

A minimal server that answers any TCP port through the tunnel and prints its tailcat address. The zero value Server picks defaults for anything unset: a fresh ephemeral key, the nearest region of the default DERP map, and logging (set to for quiet):

package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"net"

	"github.com/tailscale/tailcat"
)

func main() {
	s := &tailcat.Server{
		OnTCP: func(port uint16) func(net.Conn) {
			return func(c net.Conn) {
				fmt.Fprintf(c, "hello from port %v\n", port)
				c.Close()
			}
		},
	}
	if err := s.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(s.TailcatAddr())
	select {}
}

And a minimal client that dials it, given that tailcat address as its argument. Like Server, the Client zero value works with just its field set to a tailcat address ( is shorthand for exactly that), and the tunnel is established lazily by the first dial:

package main

import (
	"context"
	"io"
	"log"
	"os"

	"github.com/tailscale/tailcat"
)

func main() {
	cl := tailcat.NewClient(tailcat.Addr(os.Args[1]))
	defer cl.Close()
	c, err := cl.DialTCPPort(context.Background(), 80)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	io.Copy(os.Stdout, c)
}

$ ./client tcomFwWCAWf933BLELdzd3RkHiOufJ...
hello from port 80

UDP uses a connected packet connection for each client flow, preserving datagram boundaries and both endpoint addresses:

s.OnUDP = func(port uint16) func(tailcat.ConnPacketConn) {
	if port != 53 {
		return nil
	}
	return func(c tailcat.ConnPacketConn) {
		defer c.Close()
		buf := make([]byte, tailcat.MaxUDPPayload)
		for {
			n, err := c.Read(buf)
			if err != nil {
				return
			}
			c.Write(buf[:n])
		}
	}
}

pc, err := cl.DialUDPPort(context.Background(), 53)

implements both and . Keep payloads at or below (1232 bytes) to fit the IPv6 tunnel MTU without fragmentation. Use and for exit-node traffic; provides datagram-safe bidirectional forwarding. Inactive server-side UDP flows close after tailcat.DefaultUDPIdleTimeout (two minutes); set to change the timeout.

A Tailcat server is identified by a , represented by the Go type . It looks like and is a prefix followed by base64-encoded CBOR containing:

  • The server's WireGuard public key (Curve25519, 32 bytes)
  • A separate path-discovery public key (Curve25519, 32 bytes)
  • By default, an independent WireGuard pre-shared key (256 random bits), which prevents a DERP operator that observes the peers' public keys from joining the tunnel and provides post-quantum protection against recorded traffic
  • DERP info. Either:
    1. full DERP server metadata, to either use a custom DERP server, or to avoid the client needing a potential round-trip to fetch the latest DERP map (the tailcat serve --full-address flag and the subcommand produce this form)

A typical tailcat address with just an integer region ID is around 140 bytes. With embedded DERP node details it's longer but self-contained.

The default address is a secret bearer capability because it contains the pre-shared key. Share it only with clients that should be able to connect. Publishing it, in a public DNS TXT record or anywhere else, gives that capability to the whole internet, which is only safe when the server also authenticates clients: restricts the tunnel to listed client node keys, and the service requires .

Tailcat reuses Tailscale's client networking components but without the control plane.

  • -- a userspace WireGuard implementation for encrypting all tunnel traffic. It doesn't use a kernel TUN/TAP device (nor does it configure any networking routes or DNS settings), so isn't required.
  • -- Tailscale's transport layer that multiplexes traffic over direct UDP and DERP relays. It handles STUN-based endpoint discovery and UDP hole-punching for NAT traversal.
  • (gVisor) -- a userspace TCP/IP stack that terminates TCP connections inside the process. This is what lets Tailcat accept inbound connections and dial outbound ones without any OS network configuration.
  • -- Tailscale's encrypted relay protocol, used as a rendezvous channel and as a fallback data path when direct connectivity isn't possible.

  1. It generates (or loads) a WireGuard keypair and, by default, a pre-shared key, connects to a DERP relay, and prints its tailcat address to stderr. It then waits for clients.

  2. Client parses the tailcat address to learn the server's public key, path-discovery key, optional pre-shared key, and DERP region. It generates its own ephemeral keypair and connects to the same DERP relay. The separate path-discovery key can appear in cleartext direct-path disco frames without revealing the WireGuard public key. The pre-shared key remains the secret connection capability even when a relay operator observes both peers' public keys.

  3. The client sends a "" ping message to the server through the DERP relay. This message carries the client's node public key. The server receives it, adds the client to its WireGuard peer list and network map, reconfigures the WireGuard engine, and replies with a "" acknowledgment.

  4. With both sides configured as WireGuard peers using the address's pre-shared key when present, the WireGuard handshake proceeds (routed through DERP initially). Once complete, the tunnel is up and encrypted traffic can flow.

  5. In parallel, each side advertises its UDP endpoints (public IP:port learned via STUN, plus local interface addresses) to the other in disco call-me-maybe messages over DERP, re-advertising whenever they change. Both sides then run Tailscale's disco protocol and attempt UDP hole-punching. If successful, traffic upgrades from the DERP relay to a direct peer-to-peer path. If hole-punching fails, DERP continues as a fallback and the connection still works, just with rate-limited throughput if you're using our public hosted DERP relays.

  6. The client dials a TCP port on the server through the tunnel. gVisor's TCP/IP stack on both sides handles connection setup. On the server, the incoming connection is dispatched to a handler based on the port: forwarding to localhost, piping to stdout, running an SSH session, etc.

Each peer currently derives a deterministic IPv6 address from its WireGuard public key, but that's an implementation detail not exposed to end users and might change. (e.g. we might remove those bytes from the IP headers entirely and recover that redundant MTU)

See SECURITY.md for how to report security issues, and for notes on tailcat's current threat model.

Tailcat is free to use, but it comes with no API or CLI stability promises: the Go API, the CLI flags and output, and the wire format may all change. The public rate-limited Tailcat DERP relays have no uptime SLAs or throughput targets, and we may revoke access to them at any time, for any reason. Everything is provided best effort, without a contractual relationship (e.g. dedicated DERP relays and/or support) saying otherwise.

Tailcat began life in September 2023 as "derpcat", written on a long flight while catching up on bad movies: the first sketch was commit 9e4d925cc ("cmd/dc: start of derpcat tool"), and it first worked in commit 911915fbb ("derpcat: it's alive!", whose commit message notes "UA 605 PDX-ORD en route to Ireland. yay not buying the wifi."). Back then it lived inside a fork of the tailscale.com repo and it bitrot several times as the Tailscale internals moved on without it. We've since brought it back to life and refactored it to be a regular Go module client of the tailscale.com repo instead of a fork of it.

items.title: tradermonty/claude-trading-skills
items.content:
Claude Code skills for equity investors and traders — market analysis, technical charting, economic calendars, screeners, and trading strategy development.

Claude Trading Skills started as a personal project to use AI to improve my own trading process.

Claude Trading Skills is a Claude Skills-based trading workflow toolkit for time-constrained individual investors.

It is designed for investors who use long-term investing, ETFs, and dividend stocks as their core, while using disciplined swing trading as a satellite strategy when market conditions are favorable.

The goal is not to outsource buy/sell decisions to AI. The goal is to structure market review, risk management, trade planning, journaling, and continuous improvement. It is open source because the workflows, checklists, and review habits behind better trading decisions can improve through shared practice.

This is not a signal service or a promise of profitability. It is a toolkit for traders who want to build a better decision process.

The project follows a first for self, open for others stance: it is built first as a practical workflow the author uses, then shared openly for others who face similar constraints.

This repository is for educational, research, and process-improvement purposes only. It is not financial advice, investment advisory service, tax advice, legal advice, a signal service, or a broker execution platform. Trading and investing involve risk, including loss of principal. Past performance, backtests, screens, reports, and AI-generated analysis do not guarantee future results. All trading decisions, position sizing, tax/regulatory compliance, and broker usage are the user's responsibility.

The project is provided under the MIT License, .

This repository is designed for:

  • Time-constrained individual investors
  • Long-term investors who also want disciplined swing-trading upside
  • Dividend and ETF investors who want structured portfolio review
  • Traders who want to manage risk before finding trade candidates
  • Investors who want to journal and improve their decision process

It is not designed for fully automated trading, signal outsourcing, or short-term scalping.

Recommended Starting Path

New users should start with one of these operational workflows. Each link points to a machine-readable manifest under that names the exact skills, decision gates, and artifacts in order.

15-minute daily market checkmarket-breadth-analyzer, uptrend-analyzer, exposure-coach
Weekly long-term portfolio reviewportfolio-manager, kanchi-dividend-review-monitor, trader-memory-coreAlpaca required; manual CSV is a degraded fallback
Find swing candidates only when risk is allowedvcp-screener, drawdown-circuit-breaker, technical-analyst, position-sizer, trader-memory-core, pre-trade-discipline-gateFMP for screeners; local state for risk and discipline gates
Record and learn from every closed tradetrader-memory-core, signal-postmortem

New here? Follow Your First Week (日本語) from installation through a no-paid-data-API market check, first journal entry, and first weekly review.

These visual excerpts use fictional data to show the kinds of results you can review before setting up a skill. They are illustrations, not live market readings or trading instructions.

Select a preview to open the full-size SVG; on a phone, zoom after opening.

Offline Quick Start takes you from these previews to a fictional report and then the Navigator, without provider keys.

Claude Web Skills are currently available on Free, Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise accounts; see Anthropic's current Skills help because access can change. Claude Code has separate account requirements, and the Claude.ai Free plan does not include it; see the Claude Code setup guide. FMP, FINVIZ Elite, and Alpaca are optional data or broker integrations for specific workflows. The five-skill starter path below works with public CSVs, chart screenshots, and local files, so it does not require a paid market-data API subscription.

If you do not have FMP / FINVIZ / Alpaca subscriptions, start with these five skills and run them manually:

  1. — public CSV breadth scoring; no API key
  2. — public CSV uptrend participation; no API key
  3. — pure calculation; no I/O
  4. — local YAML journaling
  5. — review framework

This path lets you review market conditions, size trades, journal decisions, and review outcomes . Note: "no API" does not mean "no external data" — these skills still need public CSVs, chart screenshots, or local files. See each skill's entry in for exact input requirements.

is the authoritative index of all skills. If this README, , or docs disagree with the index, the index is correct. The same applies to multi-skill workflows — is canonical.

  • – Source folder for each trading skill. Contains , reference material, and any helper scripts.
  • – Canonical metadata index for every skill (id, category, integrations, workflows back-references).
  • – Operational workflow manifests for the Core + Satellite routines (canonical, validator-enforced via ).
  • – Pre-built archives ready to upload to Claude's web app tab.
  • – Documentation site content, generated skill pages, and docs/dev/metadata-and-workflow-schema.md (schema spec).
  • – Repository-level automation, including the schema validator and one-shot bootstrap helper.
  • – Purpose-specific install bundles defining required / recommended / optional skills for major goals (6 skillsets shipped: market-regime, core-portfolio, dividend-income, swing-opportunity, trade-memory, strategy-research; consumed by the Navigator).

First time here? Read the FAQ for plan, cost, safety, and scope answers.

  1. Open the latest GitHub Release and download the asset that matches the skill you want, plus . Verify its hash as described in the release policy. If the Releases page is empty, follow the source-folder installation path below or build a local package with scripts/package_skills.py.
  2. For an individual account, open and enable Code execution and file creation. Team and Enterprise users may need an organization owner to enable Skills.
  3. Open , upload the ZIP, confirm it appears in the list, and enable it if needed (see Anthropic's current Skills help).

Use with Claude Code (desktop or CLI)

  1. Clone or download this repository.
  2. Copy the desired skill folder (e.g., ) to for personal use or inside a project (see the Claude Code setup guide).
